```{=latex}
PREDICTING PITCH SEQUENCES IN BASEBALL USING MULTINOMIAL LOGISTIC REGRESSION

An Abstract of the Thesis by

Brian Bruxvoort
\end{singlespace}

\vspace{0.3cm}
```

This research develops multinomial logistic regression models for predicting pitch sequences in Major League Baseball using Statcast data from the 2025 regular season. Individual models were constructed for each pitcher rather than a single league-wide model, with predictors restricted to observable game state variables including pitch history, ball-strike count, batter handedness, and pitch location zone. The comprehensive model achieved 62.36% classification accuracy, substantially exceeding the 32% naive baseline. Pitcher predictability varied considerably, with relief pitchers proving systematically more predictable than starting pitchers due to their narrower repertoires and more defined roles. A joint pitch type and location model failed due to severe data sparsity created by the expansion of outcome categories. These findings offer practical implications for scouting and hitter preparation while demonstrating that classical statistical methods can effectively model sequential pitch selection patterns.

# Introduction

Baseball, often referred to as America's pastime, has evolved from a simple game of bats and balls into a complex strategic battle where every pitch matters. At the heart of this battle lies one of the game's most intriguing questions: what pitch will the pitcher throw next? This seemingly simple question has been the focus of players, coaches, and analysts for generations, as the ability to anticipate the next pitch can dramatically shift the competitive balance between hitter and pitcher.

A hitter who successfully anticipates the type and location of an incoming pitch gains precious milliseconds to react which is a critical advantage in a sport where a 95 mph fastball travels from the pitcher's hand to home plate in approximately 400 milliseconds [@boddy2012]. This competitive advantage has led to numerous controversies throughout baseball history, from traditional sign-stealing techniques to more recent scandals involving electronic devices, as exemplified by the 2017 Boston Red Sox incident where the team allegedly used Apple Watches to decode opposing catchers' signals [@stratton2018].

As technology has advanced, advanced analytics and machine learning have been introduced. Due to this advancement, the approach to understanding and predicting pitch sequences has fundamentally transformed. Modern baseball generates vast quantities of data through systems like MLB's Statcast, which tracks every pitch thrown in every game with unprecedented detail [@mlb2024]. This data revolution has created new opportunities for researchers to apply sophisticated statistical and computational methods to the age-old problem of pitch prediction.

This thesis addresses the challenge of predicting pitch sequences in Major League Baseball using multinomial logistic regression models. Unlike previous research that has focused primarily on neural networks or support vector machines, this study leverages the interpretability and efficiency of logistic regression while building individual models for each pitcher in the 2025 MLB season. By focusing on readily observable game state variables which include count, batter handedness, and pitch history, this research aims to create a practical, implementable system that could be utilized in real-time during games.

## Research Objectives

The primary objective of this research is to develop and evaluate multiple iterations of multinomial logistic regression models that predict pitch type based on easily trackable game situation variables. Rather than pursuing the absolute highest possible prediction accuracy through complex feature engineering, this study prioritizes practical usability and real-world applicability.

This research makes several contributions to the existing literature on pitch prediction. First, it provides a systematic comparison of multinomial logistic regression models with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the tradeoffs between model sophistication and prediction accuracy. Second, it builds separate models for each pitcher rather than a single league-wide model, accounting for individual pitching styles and tendencies. Third, it emphasizes practical implementation by restricting predictors to variables that are readily observable during live game situations. Finally, it provides comprehensive statistical analysis comparing model performance across different specifications, offering insights into which game state variables contribute most significantly to pitch prediction accuracy.

## Literature Review

The study of pitch sequences and pitch prediction in baseball has evolved significantly over the past two decades, driven by advances in data collection technology and analytical methodologies. This literature review examines three interconnected areas of research: the strategic importance of pitch sequences, various approaches to predicting pitch types, and the specific application of logistic regression models to this problem.

### The Strategic Role of Pitch Sequences

Clay [-@clay2023] conducted one of the most comprehensive recent studies on two-pitch sequence behavior using discrete-time Markov chains to analyze pitch location patterns. Examining data from 87 American League pitchers during the 2019 season, Clay found that pitchers could be grouped into five distinct clusters based on their two-pitch location sequence behaviors, with significant differences in performance metrics between groups. Notably, the highest-performing group included elite pitchers like Justin Verlander and Gerrit Cole, who demonstrated what Clay termed "situational variance" which as he put it, the elite pitchers varied their two-pitch sequences more than other groups in certain game situations while remaining consistent in others, particularly when beginning and ending at-bats.

Boddy [-@boddy2012] provided practical insights into pitch sequencing strategies from a training perspective, emphasizing data driven decision making in pitch selection. Drawing on large scale data mining of MLB pitches, Boddy outlined how different pitch types serve distinct strategic purposes. Fastballs establish velocity expectations and generate strikes, curveballs disrupt timing, sliders generate strikeouts, and change-ups/sinkers induce groundballs. His analysis revealed that sliders have the highest "whiff rate" while curveballs have the highest "watch rate," suggesting that pitch effectiveness depends heavily on game situation and previous pitch selection [@boddy2012].

### Machine Learning Approaches to Pitch Prediction

The application of machine learning to pitch prediction has expanded dramatically since the early 2010s, with researchers using increasingly sophisticated techniques. Ganeshapillai and Guttag [-@ganeshapillai2012] conducted work in this area as they developed linear support vector machines to predict pitch types for individual pitchers. Using data from the 2008 and 2009 MLB seasons, they built separate models for 359 pitchers, incorporating 48 features including previous pitch, count, score differential, base runners, and pitcher tendencies. Their analysis revealed that previous pitcher actions specific to the count and pitcher behavior toward specific batters were among the most important predictive features [@ganeshapillai2012].

More recent work has leveraged neural networks and deep learning architectures. Augustine [-@augustine2024] developed "MLB Pitch Predictor" using Azure Machine Learning Studio, applying a Multiclass Boosted Decision Tree algorithm to predict pitches thrown by Tyler Glasnow. After incorporating data from both 2023 and early 2024 seasons, Augustine achieved a 66% overall accuracy rate, with the model reaching 73% accuracy in specific game applications. Importantly, Augustine's work highlighted practical limitations of pitch prediction models, including a pitcher's ability to adjust strategies mid-game, park factors, umpire strike zone variability, and the fundamental unpredictability of human decision-making [@augustine2024].

Lee [-@lee2022] expanded the prediction problem beyond pitch type to simultaneously predict both pitch type and location, classifying pitches into 34 categories. Using an ensemble of deep neural networks, Lee achieved 62.4% accuracy compared to a naive baseline of 8.2%. Interestingly, Lee's analysis revealed that prediction accuracy increased in specific game situations, particularly when the pitcher's team was losing, when the count was unfavorable to the pitcher, or when a runner was in scoring position [@lee2022]. These findings suggest that pitchers become more predictable under pressure, following established patterns more closely when game situations are disadvantageous.

### Logistic Regression Models for Pitch Prediction

Despite the expansion of complex machine learning techniques, logistic regression remains relevant for pitch prediction due to its interpretability, computational efficiency, and strong performance when appropriately specified. Stratton [-@stratton2018] conducted extensive research on pitch prediction using Bayesian hierarchical multinomial regression, specifically analyzing Clayton Kershaw's pitching data from 2008 to 2014. Stratton's approach grouped pitches by catcher, recognizing that different catcher-pitcher relationships might result in different pitch calling patterns [@stratton2018].

Stratton employed a Block Metropolis-within-Gibbs sampler to estimate the hierarchical model, that predicted pitch type based on count and previous pitch type. A key finding was that the hierarchical model significantly outperformed its non-hierarchical counterpart, providing "extremely strong evidence" that accounting for catcher-specific effects improved prediction quality. The hierarchical modeling approach offers particular advantages through shrinkage estimators that "borrow information" across groups in the hierarchy, resulting in more stable estimates for catchers with limited data [@@stratton2018].

Hastie and Powers [-@hastie2011] explored the interpretability advantages of logistic regression in predicting baseball outcomes, emphasizing how regression coefficients can be directly interpreted as log-odds ratios. This interpretability allows coaches and analysts to understand not just which pitch is most likely, but why that information may be as valuable as the prediction itself [@hastie2011].

### Research Gaps and Present Study

While existing research has made substantial progress in understanding and predicting pitch sequences, several gaps remain. First, much of the recent research has focused on maximizing prediction accuracy through complex neural networks, sometimes at the expense of practical implementability and interpretability. Second, many studies have built league-wide models rather than pitcher-specific models, potentially missing important individual differences in pitching strategy. Third, few studies have systematically compared models of increasing complexity to identify the optimal balance between sophistication and performance.

This thesis addresses these gaps in a few ways. The first is developing multinomial logistic regression models that prioritize practical usability while maintaining competitive accuracy. Second, it builds separate models for each pitcher to account for individual tendencies and styles. Third, it systematically compares five model specifications of increasing complexity to identify which additional features provide meaningful improvements in prediction accuracy. Lastly, it uses only variables that are readily observable during live games, ensuring the models could be implemented in real-time situations.

# Data

The foundation of this research is Statcast data from the 2025 Major League Baseball regular season, obtained through the MLB's BaseballSavant website. Statcast is MLB's official tracking technology, using high-resolution cameras and radar equipment to record detailed information about every pitch, swing, and play across all MLB games.

Due to BaseballSavant's limitations on quantity of exportable pitch data, the pitch data for each individual team was exported individually. BaseballSavant limits the user to exporting a maximum of 25,000 rows (pitches) of data. Thankfully, each team threw no more than 25,000 pitches throughout the 2025 season. After the pitch data for each team was exported, they were then combined into one dataset using joins so that the analysis could be completed.

The newly created raw dataset contained 118 variables capturing diverse aspects of each pitch, including pitch velocity, spin rate, release point coordinates, pitch movement characteristics, batted ball outcomes, and contextual game state information. The complete dataset comprised 712,528 individual pitch observations, which represents the total number of pitches thrown across all MLB games during the 2025 regular season.

## Variable Selection

For the purposes of this research, a subset of variables was selected based on two primary criteria. The first was relevance to pitch prediction modeling, and the second was practical observability during live game situations. The following variables were retained for analysis:

- **pitch_type**: The classification of pitch type (e.g., four-seam fastball, slider, curveball)
- **player_name**: The name of the pitcher
- **zone**: The pitch location zone within or around the strike zone (14 distinct zones)
- **stand**: Batter handedness (left-handed or right-handed)
- **balls**: The number of balls in the current count
- **strikes**: The number of strikes in the current count
- **at_bat_number**: Sequential identifier for the at-bat within the game

This variable selection strategy reflects a deliberate emphasis on model interpretability and practical implementation. While more sophisticated feature engineering incorporating variables such as spin axis, release height, or pitch movement characteristics could potentially enhance predictive accuracy, such an approach introduces several complications. First, these variables are not readily observable during live games without specialized equipment. Second, extensive feature engineering increases the risk of model overfitting. Third, many of the 118 available variables exhibit substantial multicollinearity. For instance, spin axis, velocity, and horizontal/vertical break are all interrelated and collectively determine pitch type.

By restricting the analysis to basic, observable game state variables, this research prioritizes the development of models that are simultaneously interpretable, computationally efficient, and implementable in real-time game contexts.

## Descriptive Statistics

Before getting into the modeling and analysis, exploratory analysis of the 2025 MLB pitch data was completed to examine the distribution of key variables and identifying patterns that will inform the modeling approach.

### Pitch Type Distribution

```{r fig.cap="Distribution of Pitch Types in 2025 MLB Season"}
pitch_type_summary <- pitch_data %>%
  count(pitch_type) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

ggplot(pitch_type_summary, aes(x = reorder(pitch_type, -n), y = n, fill = pitch_type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, "\n(", round(percentage, 1), "%)")), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.5) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Pitch Types", subtitle = paste("Total pitches:", sum(pitch_type_summary$n)), x = "Pitch Type", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

The pitch type abbreviations used in this paper are defined as follows:

- **CH** - Changeup
- **CU** - Curveball
- **FC** - Cutter
- **EP** - Eephus
- **FO** - Forkball
- **FF** - Four-Seam Fastball
- **KN** - Knuckleball
- **KC** - Knuckle-curve
- **SC** - Screwball
- **SI** - Sinker
- **SL** - Slider
- **SV** - Slurve
- **FS** - Splitter
- **ST** - Sweeper

Figure 2.1 displays the frequency distribution of pitch types across all 712,528 pitches in the dataset. Four-seam fastballs (FF) dominate MLB pitching, accounting for 231,059 pitches (31.7% of all pitches thrown). Sinkers (SI) represent the second-most common pitch type with 110,593 pitches (15.5%), followed by sliders (SL) at 104,875 pitches (14.7%) and changeups (CH) at 73,074 pitches (10.3%).

The dominance of fastballs/sinkers and the relative frequency of other pitch types establish a baseline expectation: any effective prediction model should at minimum perform better than a naive baseline that always predicts the most common pitch type. Such a baseline would achieve 31.7% accuracy if fastballs were the only predicted pitch, which is a benchmark that contextualizes future model performance.

### Zone Distribution

```{r fig.cap="Distribution of Pitch Locations Across Strike Zones"}
zone_summary <- pitch_data %>%
  count(zone) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%
  arrange(desc(n))

ggplot(zone_summary, aes(x = reorder(zone, -n), y = n, fill = factor(zone))) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, "\n(", round(percentage, 1), "%)")), vjust = -0.5, size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Pitch Zones", subtitle = paste("Total pitches:", sum(zone_summary$n)), x = "Zone", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 0.5))
```

![Strike Zone Layout with 14 Zones](pitch_zones.png){fig-cap="Strike Zone Layout with 14 Zones" fig-align="center" width="50%"}
\begin{center}
\textit{Note: The zone graphic is from the catcher/umpire's point of view.}
\end{center}

Figure 2.2 illustrates the spatial distribution of pitches across the 14 defined strike zones. Zone 14, representing pitches outside and off the plate, contains the highest frequency of pitches at (17.8%). The distribution reveals that approximately 60% of pitches are thrown within the official strike zone (zones 1-9), with the remaining 40% thrown outside the zone.

### Count Distribution

```{r fig.cap="Distribution of Ball-Strike Counts"}
count_summary <- pitch_data %>%
  count(balls, strikes) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100, count_label = paste0(balls, "-", strikes)) %>%
  arrange(balls, strikes)

ggplot(count_summary, aes(x = factor(strikes), y = factor(balls), fill = n)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", size = 1) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, "\n(", round(percentage, 1), "%)")), color = "white", size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#3B4CC0", high = "#B40426", name = "Count") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Pitch Counts (Balls-Strikes)", x = "Strikes", y = "Balls") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), axis.text = element_text(size = 11), panel.grid = element_blank())
```

Figure 2.4 presents the frequency distribution of all possible ball-strike count combinations. The most common count is 0-0 (183,362 pitches, 25.7%), which necessarily appears at the beginning of every plate appearance. Two-strike counts collectively account for approximately 30% of all pitches, while full counts (3-2) occur with moderate frequency (35,841 pitches, 5.0%).

### Batter Handedness

```{r fig.cap="Batter Handedness Distribution"}
stand_summary <- pitch_data %>%
  count(stand) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100,
         stand_label = case_when(
           stand == "R" ~ "Right-Handed",
           stand == "L" ~ "Left-Handed",
           TRUE ~ as.character(stand))) %>% arrange(desc(n))

ggplot(stand_summary, aes(x = "", y = n, fill = stand_label)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 1) +
  coord_polar("y", start = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(stand_label, "\n", n, "\n(", round(percentage, 1), "%)")), position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 5, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Left-Handed" = "#2E86AB", "Right-Handed" = "#A23B72")) +
  labs(title = "Batter Handedness Distribution (Pie Chart)") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14, hjust = 0.5), legend.position = "none")
```

Figure 2.5 displays the distribution of batter handedness. Right-handed batters faced 394,796 pitches (55.4%), while left-handed batters faced 317,732 pitches (44.6%). This approximate 55-45 split ensures sufficient data to estimate handedness-specific effects with reasonable precision.

### Pitch Sequences

```{r fig.cap="Top 15 Most Common Two-Pitch Sequences"}
pitch_sequences <- pitch_data1 %>%
  arrange(pitcher, game_date, at_bat_number, pitch_number) %>%
  group_by(pitcher, game_date, at_bat_number) %>%
  mutate(prev_pitch = lag(pitch_type)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  filter(!is.na(prev_pitch)) %>%
  count(prev_pitch, pitch_type) %>%
  group_by(prev_pitch) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%
  ungroup()

top_sequences <- pitch_sequences %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  head(15) %>%
  mutate(sequence = paste(prev_pitch, "→", pitch_type))

ggplot(top_sequences, aes(x = reorder(sequence, n), y = n, fill = sequence)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, " (", round(percentage, 1), "%)")), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Most Common Pitch Sequences", x = "Pitch Sequence", y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)))
```

Figure 2.6 presents the 15 most frequently observed two-pitch sequences, sorted by raw count. It is important to note that the percentages shown reflect conditional probabilities rather than overall proportions as each percentage represents how often a given pitch type follows the first pitch in that sequence, not the sequence's share of all pitches thrown. For example, FF→FF occurring 73,078 times with a 43.1% label means that after a four-seam fastball is thrown, pitchers follow it with another four-seam fastball 43.1% of the time. Other frequent patterns include sinker-sinker sequences (28,659 times, 36%), meaning sinkers are followed by another sinker 36% of the time, slider-slider sequences (27,518 times, 35.3%), and fastball-slider sequences (25,375 times, 15%). Because the percentages are conditioned on different first pitches, they cannot be directly compared across sequences, which is why the graph is ordered by count rather than percentage.

### Pitch Type by Zone

```{r fig.cap="Top 15 Most Common Pitch Type-Zone Combinations"}
pitch_zone_summary <- pitch_data1 %>%
  count(pitch_type, zone) %>%
  group_by(pitch_type) %>%
  mutate(percentage = n / sum(n) * 100) %>%
  ungroup()
top_pitch_zone <- pitch_zone_summary %>%
  arrange(desc(n)) %>%
  head(15) %>%
  mutate(combination = paste(pitch_type, "- Zone", zone))
ggplot(top_pitch_zone, aes(x = reorder(combination, n), y = n, fill = pitch_type)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", show.legend = TRUE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0(n, " (", round(percentage, 1), "%)")), hjust = -0.1, size = 3.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Top 15 Most Common Pitch Type-Zone Combinations", x = "Pitch Type - Zone", y = "Count", fill = "Pitch Type") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)))
```

Figure 2.7 displays the most frequently observed combinations of pitch type and pitch location zone, sorted by raw count. As with Figure 2.6, the percentages shown are conditional which means each percentage represents how often a given pitch type is thrown to that particular zone relative to all locations that pitch type is thrown, not the combination's share of all pitches. For example, fastballs thrown to zone 11 represent the single most common pitch-location combination (38,897 times), meaning that of all four-seam fastballs thrown, that percentage land in zone 11 which is consistent with the newer yet conventional strategy of "elevating the fastball." Sliders appear most frequently in zone 14 (outside off the plate, 31,034 occurrences), reflecting their strategic use as "chase" pitches, with that percentage of all sliders being thrown to that location. Changeups concentrate in zones 13 and 14 (low and outside), corresponding to their designed downward movement to induce groundballs. Because percentages are conditioned on each individual pitch type, they cannot be directly compared across different pitch types, which is why the graph is ordered by count rather than percentage.

# Methodology

This chapter describes the analytical approach employed to predict pitch sequences in Major League Baseball. The research design emphasizes practical implementation and model interpretability while maintaining competitive predictive accuracy.

## Research Design

This research uses a quantitative, predictive modeling approach analyzing pitch sequencing in the 2025 MLB season. Rather than building a single league-wide model, the analytical strategy constructs individual multinomial logistic regression models for each pitcher who threw a sufficient number of pitches during the season.

The research design follows a systematic model comparison framework, evaluating five distinct model specifications of increasing complexity. Each successive model adds additional predictor variables, allowing assessment of whether increased complexity yields proportionate improvements in predictive accuracy. Model performance is evaluated using classification accuracy as the primary metric as the proportion of pitches correctly predicted.

## Theoretical Framework

### Multinomial Logistic Regression Framework

Multinomial logistic regression extends binary logistic regression to accommodate outcome variables with more than two categories. In this application, the outcome variable is pitch type, which can take on multiple values (fastball, slider, curveball, changeup, etc.). The model estimates the probability of each possible pitch type conditional on the observed predictor variables.

For an observation *i* with predictor vector **X**_*i*, the probability that the outcome falls into category *j* is modeled as:

$$P(Y_i = j | \mathbf{X}_i) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^{J} \exp(\mathbf{X}_i \boldsymbol{\beta}_k)}$$

where *J* represents the total number of pitch type categories, and **β**_*j* represents the coefficient vector associated with category *j*. This formulation ensures that predicted probabilities sum to 1 across all categories.

The model estimates *J*-1 sets of coefficients, with one category serving as the reference group. Coefficients can be interpreted as log-odds ratios. Bascially, a one-unit increase in predictor *X* changes the log-odds of observing pitch type *j* relative to the reference category by β_*j*.

### Methodological Innovation: Lagged Variables

A key contribution of this research is demonstrating how multinomial logistic regression can be adapted for sequential prediction through careful incorporation of lagged variables. This combination addresses a methodological gap in some previous pitch prediction research.

Multinomial logistic regression is optimal for unordered categorical outcomes, like what is being predicted here. It produces interpretable probability distributions rather than hard classifications, and offers coefficient interpretability through log-odds ratios. Unlike neural networks, the model structure remains transparent, allowing analysts to understand why specific predictions are made.

Pitch selection is inherently sequential as pitchers use previous pitches to "set up" subsequent pitches. Lagged variables (lag1_pitch_type, lag2_pitch_type, lag1_zone, lag2_zone) implement this sequential dependency by including previous pitches as predictors.

Combining categorical lagged variables with multinomial logistic regression introduces several challenges. The first is parameter expansion as each categorical lag requires multiple indicator variables. Another is at-bat boundary handling as sequences segment at at-bat boundaries. And finally, multiple lag types as this requires the model to learn multi-dimensional sequential patterns. This research demonstrates that classical statistical methods can successfully incorporate sequential dependencies while maintaining interpretability and computational efficiency.

### Alternative Approaches Considered

During model development, random forest and XGBoost models were constructed and evaluated using the same predictor variables and training data. However, after initial testing, it was revealed that these sophisticated algorithms provided no meaningful improvement in classification accuracy compared to multinomial logistic regression. Random forest models achieved accuracy to that of logistic regression models, but it required substantially greater computational resources.

This result makes intuitive sense as pitch selection is fundamentally a linear decision process influenced by readily identifiable factors. When the underlying data-generating process is approximately linear, simpler models often match or exceed the performance of complex alternatives while offering superior interpretability.

## Model Specifications

Five distinct model specifications were developed and evaluated, each incorporating different combinations of predictor variables. All models use the same underlying multinomial logistic regression framework, differing only in the predictors included.

The models were developed through an iterative process. Model 3 (Basic Model) was created first as a comprehensive "kitchen sink" approach including all readily observable predictors. Following this baseline, Models 4 and 5 explored alternative ways of modeling the relationship between pitch type and location using interactions and interaction variables. Finally, Models 1 and 2 were developed to test whether simpler specifications could achieve comparable accuracy, while favoring low computational capabilities and ease of implementation.

### Model 1: Simple Model

The first model specification represents the minimal viable approach to pitch prediction, incorporating only information about recent pitch history and position within the at-bat.

**Predictor variables:**

- lag1_pitch_type: The type of pitch thrown immediately before the current pitch

- lag2_pitch_type: The type of pitch thrown two pitches ago

- pitch_number: The sequential number of the current pitch within the at-bat

This specification tests whether simple pitch sequencing patterns alone provide meaningful predictive information.

### Model 2: Simple Model with Batter Handedness

The second model extends Model 1 but adds batter handedness:

**Predictor variables:**

- All variables from Model 1

- stand: Whether the batter bats left-handed or right-handed

This addition allows the model to capture platoon related adjustments in pitch selection. This is important as certain pitches move more effectively against same-handed versus opposite-handed batters, not to mention a pitcher's strategy changes based on the whether the batter is left-handed or right-handed.

### Model 3: Basic Model with Count and Zone

Model 3 adds onto model 2 but incorporates count information and pitch location history:

**Predictor variables:**

- All variables from Model 2

- balls: Number of balls in the current count

- strikes: Number of strikes in the current count

- lag1_zone: The pitch location zone of the previous pitch

- lag2_zone: The pitch location zone two pitches ago

Count variables capture the strategic dynamic where pitchers facing favorable counts possess greater freedom to throw pitches outside the strike zone, while unfavorable counts necessitate throwing strikes.

### Model 4: Separate Type and Zone Models

The fourth approach constructs two separate models rather than a single integrated model to try to predict the next pitch type and the next pitch location:

- **Type Model**: Predicts only pitch type using all predictor variables
- **Zone Model**: Predicts only pitch location using all predictor variables

Both models employ the same predictor set but optimize predictions for their respective outcomes independently. Overall accuracy is computed as the proportion of pitches where both type and zone are predicted correctly.

### Model 5: Interaction Model

This model treats pitch type and location as a single joint outcome, predicting specific type-zone combinations rather than modeling them separately.

**Predictor variables:**

- lag1_pitch_type: Previous pitch type

- lag1_zone: Previous pitch zone  

- balls: Current ball count

- strikes: Current strike count

- stand: Batter handedness

Rather than predicting pitch type alone (e.g., "slider"), this model predicts the specific combination (e.g., "slider in zone 14"). This creates a much larger number of outcome categories (potentially 100+ combinations) but captures the interdependence between type and location decisions.

## Model Training and Evaluation

### Data Preparation

As explained earlier, prior to model training, lagged variables were constructed by shifting pitch sequence data within each at-bat. It was made sure that lag variables did not carry over between at-bats meaning the first pitch of each at-bat has no previous pitch, so lag variables are coded as "None."

Categorical variables were properly encoded for inclusion in regression models, with one category designated as the reference level. Observations with missing data for key variables were removed, though the missing data was minimal with less than 0.5% of observations.

### Model Fitting Process

For each pitcher who threw more than a minimum threshold of pitches of 100, individual models were fit using that pitcher's data exclusively. Model fitting uses maximum likelihood estimation implemented through the `nnet` package in R.

The fitting process proceeds iteratively. Starting with initial coefficient estimates, the algorithm computes predicted probabilities, calculates the gradient of the log-likelihood function, and updates coefficients in the direction that increases likelihood. This process repeats until convergence, defined as minimal change in coefficients between iterations.

### Performance Evaluation

Classification accuracy is computed as:

$$\text{Accuracy} = \frac{\text{Number of Correct Predictions}}{\text{Total Number of Predictions}}$$

For each pitch, the model generates predicted probabilities for each possible pitch type. The predicted pitch type is the category with the highest probability. A naive baseline model that always predicts the most common pitch type would achieve accuracy equal to that pitch type's frequency that as discussed earlier, is typically around 30-35%.

## Statistical Comparison of Models

To compare the performance of each model to one another, a few methods were implemented including pairwise comparisons, analysis of variance, and effect size calculations.

### Pairwise Comparisons

Model performance was compared using paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, which account for the fact that multiple models make predictions for the same pitchers. Both tests provided p-values indicating the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis of no difference.

### Analysis of Variance

Overall differences across all five models were assessed using one-way repeated measures ANOVA. Following a significant ANOVA result, Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference post-hoc test identified which specific model pairs differ significantly.

### Effect Size Calculation

Cohen's d was calculated for each significant pairwise comparison:

$$d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{\text{pooled}}}$$

Cohen's d values of 0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 are conventionally interpreted as small, medium, and large effect sizes, respectively.

## Computational Implementation

All data processing, model fitting, and analysis were conducted using R (version 4.3.1 or later). Key packages employed include tidyverse, nnet, caret, and knitr. Total computational time for fitting all five model specifications across all pitchers was approximately 2-4 hours on a computer with standard capabilites.

```{r}
# Model 1: Simple (2 previous pitches + pitch number)
model1_models <- readRDS("pitcher_models_simple.rds")
model1_data <- readRDS("pitch_data_features_simple.rds")
model1_evals <- readRDS("model_evaluations_simple.rds")

# Model 2: Simple with Stand
model2_models <- readRDS("pitcher_models_simple_stand.rds")
model2_data <- readRDS("pitch_data_features_simple_stand.rds")
model2_evals <- readRDS("model_evaluations_simple_stand.rds")

# Model 3: Basic with count and zone
model3_models <- readRDS("pitcher_models_basic.rds")
model3_data <- readRDS("pitch_data_features_basic.rds")
model3_evals <- readRDS("model_evaluations_basic.rds")

# Model 4: Separate type and zone models
model4_type_models <- readRDS("pitcher_type_models_separate.rds")
model4_zone_models <- readRDS("pitcher_zone_models_separate.rds")
model4_data <- readRDS("pitch_data_features_separate.rds")
```
