# Results

This chapter presents the performance evaluation and comparative analysis of the five multinomial logistic regression model specifications. Results are organized into four major sections: overall model performance comparison, statistical significance testing, pitcher-specific performance patterns, and model complexity analysis. Findings reveal substantial differences in predictive accuracy across model specifications and considerable variation in predictability across individual pitchers.

## Overall Model Performance

```{r}
extract_accuracy <- function(eval_list, model_name, model_type = "Combined") {
  if (is.data.frame(eval_list)) {
    return(eval_list %>%
             mutate(model = model_name, model_type = model_type))
  }
  accuracy_df <- data.frame(
    pitcher = names(eval_list),
    accuracy = sapply(eval_list, function(x) {
      if (is.list(x)) {
        if ("combined_accuracy" %in% names(x)) {
          return(x$combined_accuracy)
        } else if ("accuracy" %in% names(x)) {
          return(x$accuracy)
        } else {
          return(NA)
        }
      } else if (is.numeric(x)) {
        return(x)
      } else {
        return(NA)
      }
    }),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  accuracy_df <- accuracy_df %>%
    mutate(model = model_name, model_type = model_type) %>%
    select(model, model_type, pitcher, accuracy)
  
  return(accuracy_df)
}

model1_accuracy <- extract_accuracy(model1_evals, "Model 1: Simple")
model2_accuracy <- extract_accuracy(model2_evals, "Model 2: Simple + Stand")
model3_accuracy <- extract_accuracy(model3_evals, "Model 3: Basic")
model4_type_accuracy <- extract_accuracy(model4_type_evals, "Model 4: Separate", "Type Only")
model4_zone_accuracy <- extract_accuracy(model4_zone_evals, "Model 4: Separate", "Zone Only")
model5_accuracy <- extract_accuracy(model5_evals, "Model 5: Interaction")

all_accuracies <- bind_rows(
  model1_accuracy,
  model2_accuracy,
  model3_accuracy,
  model4_type_accuracy,
  model4_zone_accuracy,
  model5_accuracy)

model4_approx_combined <- all_accuracies %>%
  filter(model == "Model 4: Separate") %>%
  select(pitcher, model_type, accuracy) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = model_type, values_from = accuracy) %>%
  mutate(accuracy = `Type Only` * `Zone Only`, model = "Model 4: Separate", model_type = "Combined (Approximated)") %>%
  select(model, model_type, pitcher, accuracy)

all_accuracies <- bind_rows(all_accuracies, model4_approx_combined)
```

### Summary Statistics

```{r}
overall_model_stats <- all_accuracies %>%
  mutate(model_combined = ifelse(model == "Model 4: Separate", paste(model, "-", model_type), model)) %>%
  filter(!model_combined %in% c("Model 4: Separate - Type Only", "Model 4: Separate - Zone Only")) %>%
  group_by(model_combined) %>%
  summarise(
    n_pitchers = n(),
    mean_accuracy = mean(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_accuracy = median(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_accuracy = sd(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_accuracy))

knitr::kable(overall_model_stats,
             col.names = c("Model", "N Pitchers", "Mean Accuracy", "Median Accuracy", "SD"),
             digits = 4,
             caption = "Overall Model Performance Summary")
```

Table 4.1 displays the distribution of classification accuracy across all pitchers for each of the five model configurations. Model 3 (Basic) achieved the highest mean accuracy at 62.36% (median = 57.82%, SD = 0.1797), making it the best performing model for predicting pitch type. This result is particularly notable given that Model 4's Type Only component, which uses an identical predictor structure to Model 3 but is optimized solely for pitch type prediction, achieved a mean accuracy of 62.38%, which was a difference of only 0.02 percentage points. Because these two models are functionally equivalent for pitch type prediction, Model 4's Type Only output was excluded from this table to avoid redundancy. Instead, Model 4 is represented here by its approximated combined accuracy, which reflects its intended purpose of jointly predicting both pitch type and location.

The simple models (Models 1 and 2) achieved substantially lower accuracy than Model 3. Model 1 (Simple) reached 47.20% mean accuracy (median = 46.37%, SD = 0.1125), while Model 2 (Simple + Stand) improved to 49.75% (median = 49.41%, SD = 0.1070). The addition of batter handedness to the simple model yielded a modest but consistent improvement of 2.55 percentage points, suggesting that platoon considerations contribute meaningfully to pitch selection even in the absence of count information. The similar standard deviations between Models 1 and 2 indicate that adding batter handedness improves accuracy consistently across pitchers rather than benefiting only a subset.

Model 4 (Separate - Combined Approximated) achieved a mean accuracy of 34.32% (median = 18.94%, SD = 0.3044), representing the estimated probability of correctly predicting both pitch type and location zone simultaneously. This figure is an approximation calculated by multiplying each pitcher's Type Only and Zone Only accuracies under the assumption that the two predictions are independent meaning the true combined accuracy would require raw per-pitch prediction data. The extremely large standard deviation (0.3044) and the stark gap between the mean (34.32%) and median (18.94%) indicate severe right-skew in the distribution. This indicates most pitchers have quite low combined accuracy, while a small number of pitchers with highly predictable tendencies in both type and location achieve much higher combined scores. This wide variability reflects the compounding nature of joint prediction as a pitcher must be predictable in both dimensions simultaneously to achieve a high combined accuracy.

Model 5 (Interaction) performed substantially worse than all other specifications, achieving only 23.10% mean accuracy (median = 21.30%, SD = 0.0811). This poor performance reflects the fundamental challenge of predicting joint type-zone outcomes within a single model, where the vast increase of outcome categories (over 100 possible pitch type and zone combinations) creates severe data sparsity. With many type-zone combinations occurring only rarely in a pitcher's season, the model struggles to learn reliable patterns for infrequent events. The narrow standard deviation relative to its mean indicates that this failure is consistent across pitchers, suggesting a structural limitation of the approach rather than a pitcher-specific issue.

### Visualization of Model Performance

```{r fig.cap="Model Accuracy Comparison Across All Pitchers"}
accuracies_filtered <- all_accuracies %>%
  filter(!(model == "Model 4: Separate" & model_type %in% c("Type Only", "Zone Only")))

model_summary_stats <- accuracies_filtered %>%
  group_by(model, model_type) %>%
  summarise(mean_accuracy = mean(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(accuracies_filtered, aes(x = reorder(paste(model, model_type, sep = " - "), accuracy, FUN = median), y = accuracy, fill = model)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.3, size = 1) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Model Accuracy Comparison (Box Plots)", subtitle = "Distribution of accuracy across all pitchers", x = "Model", y = "Accuracy", fill = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), legend.position = "none")
```

Figure 4.1 presents boxplots showing substantial variation both across models and within models across different pitchers. The simple models (Models 1 and 2) show relatively narrow, concentrated distributions centered around 45–50% accuracy. This tight clustering indicates that these models perform consistently across pitchers. While absolute accuracy is moderate, the models are reliable in producing similar accuracy regardless of the pitcher being modeled. The limited spread likely reflects these models' reliance on pitch sequencing patterns and batter handedness, which exhibit moderate consistency across pitchers. The interquartile ranges for both models are similarly compact, and the jittered points confirm that few pitchers fall far outside the central tendency.

Model 3 (Basic) displays a much broader distribution, with substantial spread spanning from approximately 30% to over 90% accuracy. This wide variation indicates that the comprehensive model performs very well for some pitchers but struggles with others. The large interquartile range and long right tail suggest that count and location information is highly informative for a subset of pitchers. That subset of pitchers are likely those with strong, consistent tendencies tied to game state, while providing less benefit for pitchers whose selection patterns are less structured. The median sits near 57.82%, but the broad spread of jittered points above 75% confirms that a meaningful number of pitchers are highly predictable under this model.

Model 4 (Separate - Combined Approximated) exhibits the widest distribution of any model, with a very low median near 18.94% but a long right tail extending all the way to 1.0. The interquartile box sits at the low end of the accuracy range, yet the scatter of jittered points across the full range illustrates the high variability inherent in multiplying two independent accuracy values. Pitchers who are simultaneously predictable in both pitch type and location achieve very high combined scores, while those with only moderate accuracy in either dimension see their combined score drop substantially due to the multiplicative penalty.

Model 5 (Interaction) shows a narrow distribution concentrated at low accuracy values around 20–25%, with virtually no observations above 40%, confirming that the fundamental structural limitation of joint type-zone prediction affects all pitchers similarly regardless of individual tendencies. The tight clustering here mirrors Models 1 and 2 in spread, but at a far lower accuracy level.

```{r fig.cap="Accuracy Distribution by Model"}
accuracies_filtered <- accuracies_filtered %>%
  mutate(model_label = paste(model, model_type, sep = " - "))

model_summary_stats <- accuracies_filtered %>%
  group_by(model_label) %>%
  summarise(mean_accuracy = mean(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(accuracies_filtered, aes(x = accuracy, fill = model_label)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_vline(data = model_summary_stats, aes(xintercept = mean_accuracy, color = model_label), linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  labs(title = "Accuracy Distribution by Model", subtitle = "Dashed lines indicate mean accuracy for each model", x = "Accuracy", y = "Density", fill = "Model", color = "Model") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "vertical", legend.text = element_text(size = 8)) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 3), color = guide_legend(nrow = 3)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)))
```

Figure 4.2's density plots further illustrate the distributional differences across models. Model 5 (Interaction) shows a sharp, narrow peak around 0.20–0.25, confirming consistently poor performance across pitchers with little variation. Model 4 (Separate - Combined Approximated) displays a similarly left-skewed distribution with high density at low accuracy values and a long flat tail extending toward 1.0. Models 1 and 2 show moderately tight distributions centered around 0.47 and 0.50 respectively, with their mean lines closely aligned with their density peaks. Model 3 (Basic) exhibits the broadest and most spread out distribution, with its mean at 0.6236, reflecting the wide variation in how well the full model captures individual pitcher tendencies. The separation between the dashed mean lines across models visually confirms the performance hierarchy established in Table 4.1.

## Statistical Significance Testing

```{r}
accuracy_comparison <- accuracies_filtered %>%
  filter(model_type %in% c("Combined", "Combined (Approximated)")) %>%
  select(model, pitcher, accuracy)

common_pitchers <- accuracy_comparison %>%
  group_by(pitcher) %>%
  summarise(n_models = n_distinct(model), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(n_models >= 4) %>%
  pull(pitcher)

accuracy_comparison <- accuracy_comparison %>%
  filter(pitcher %in% common_pitchers)

models_to_compare <- unique(accuracy_comparison$model)
n_models <- length(models_to_compare)

pairwise_results <- data.frame()

for (i in 1:(n_models-1)) {
  for (j in (i+1):n_models) {
    model1_name <- models_to_compare[i]
    model2_name <- models_to_compare[j]

    model1_data <- accuracy_comparison %>%
      filter(model == model1_name) %>%
      arrange(pitcher)

    model2_data <- accuracy_comparison %>%
      filter(model == model2_name) %>%
      arrange(pitcher)

    common <- intersect(model1_data$pitcher, model2_data$pitcher)

    if (length(common) >= 10) {
      model1_acc_common <- model1_data %>%
        filter(pitcher %in% common) %>%
        arrange(pitcher) %>%
        pull(accuracy)

      model2_acc_common <- model2_data %>%
        filter(pitcher %in% common) %>%
        arrange(pitcher) %>%
        pull(accuracy)

      if (length(model1_acc_common) == length(model2_acc_common)) {
        t_test_result <- tryCatch({
          t.test(model1_acc_common, model2_acc_common, paired = TRUE)
        }, error = function(e) NULL)

        wilcox_result <- tryCatch({
          wilcox.test(model1_acc_common, model2_acc_common, paired = TRUE)
        }, error = function(e) NULL)

        mean_diff <- mean(model1_acc_common - model2_acc_common)

        if (!is.null(t_test_result) && !is.null(wilcox_result)) {
          pairwise_results <- rbind(pairwise_results, data.frame(
            Model_1 = model1_name,
            Model_2 = model2_name,
            n_pitchers = length(common),
            mean_diff = mean_diff,
            t_statistic = t_test_result$statistic,
            t_p_value = t_test_result$p.value,
            wilcox_p_value = wilcox_result$p.value,
            significant_05 = ifelse(t_test_result$p.value < 0.05, "Yes", "No"),
            significant_01 = ifelse(t_test_result$p.value < 0.01, "Yes", "No")
          ))
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

```{r fig.cap="Pairwise Statistical Significance Tests Between Models"}
if (nrow(pairwise_results) > 0) {
  knitr::kable(pairwise_results,
               col.names = c("Model 1", "Model 2", "N Pitchers", "Mean Diff",
                             "t-statistic", "t-test p-value", "Wilcoxon p-value",
                             "Sig. (α=0.05)", "Sig. (α=0.01)"),
               digits = 4,
               caption = "Pairwise Statistical Significance Tests Between Models")

  anova_result <- aov(accuracy ~ model, data = accuracy_comparison)
  anova_summary <- summary(anova_result)
  print(anova_summary)

  tukey_result <- TukeyHSD(anova_result)
  print(tukey_result)

  ggplot(pairwise_results, aes(x = paste(Model_1, "\nvs\n", Model_2), y = mean_diff, fill = significant_05)) +
    geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("No" = "gray", "Yes" = "red"), name = "Significant\n(α=0.05)") +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(title = "Mean Accuracy Difference Between Model Pairs", subtitle = "Positive values mean Model 1 performs better", x = "Model Comparison", y = "Mean Accuracy Difference") +
    theme_minimal() +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))

  for (i in 1:nrow(pairwise_results)) {
    if (pairwise_results$significant_05[i] == "Yes") {
      model1_name <- pairwise_results$Model_1[i]
      model2_name <- pairwise_results$Model_2[i]

      model1_data <- accuracy_comparison %>%
        filter(model == model1_name) %>%
        arrange(pitcher)

      model2_data <- accuracy_comparison %>%
        filter(model == model2_name) %>%
        arrange(pitcher)

      common <- intersect(model1_data$pitcher, model2_data$pitcher)

      model1_acc <- model1_data %>% filter(pitcher %in% common) %>% pull(accuracy)
      model2_acc <- model2_data %>% filter(pitcher %in% common) %>% pull(accuracy)

      pooled_sd <- sqrt((sd(model1_acc)^2 + sd(model2_acc)^2) / 2)
      cohens_d <- (mean(model1_acc) - mean(model2_acc)) / pooled_sd

      cat(paste0(model1_name, " vs ", model2_name, ": Cohen's d = ", round(cohens_d, 3), "\n"))
      if (abs(cohens_d) < 0.2) cat("  Effect size: Small\n")
      else if (abs(cohens_d) < 0.5) cat("  Effect size: Medium\n")
      else cat("  Effect size: Large\n")
    }
  }
}
```

### Analysis of Variance Results

One-way ANOVA testing for overall differences across the five model configurations revealed extremely strong evidence of performance differences (F(4, 3659) = 483.2, p < 2×10^-16^). This highly significant result confirms that model specification substantially affects prediction accuracy, with differences far too large to be attributable to chance variation. The large F-statistic and near-zero p-value confirm that at least some models differ meaningfully in performance, validating the model comparison approach and justifying proceeding to pairwise comparisons.

### Tukey's HSD Post-Hoc Comparisons

Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference test, which controls family-wise error rate across multiple comparisons, identified significant differences for all ten possible model pairs. Every pairwise comparison yielded p-values well below 0.05, indicating that each model's performance differs significantly from every other model's performance. Here are seven of the notable model comparisons.

**Model 1 vs. Model 2** (Simple vs. Simple + Stand): Model 2 outperformed Model 1 by 2.54 percentage points on average (95% CI: [0.004, 0.050], p = 0.045). This difference, while statistically significant, represents a modest improvement. The narrow confidence interval indicates reasonable precision in this estimate.

**Model 1 vs. Model 3** (Simple vs. Basic):  Model 3 outperformed Model 1 by 15.16 percentage points on average (95% CI: [0.127, 0.177], p < 0.001). This substantial difference demonstrates the considerable value of incorporating count and location information, representing a roughly 32% relative improvement over Model 1's baseline accuracy.

**Model 2 vs. Model 3** (Simple + Stand vs. Basic): Model 3 outperformed Model 2 by 12.62 percentage points (95% CI: [0.101, 0.151], p < 0.001). This isolates the contribution of count and location information beyond what simple sequencing and handedness provide, demonstrating that game state information adds substantial predictive value.

**Model 1 vs. Model 4** (Simple vs. Separate - Combined Approximated): Model 1 outperformed Model 4 by 12.88 percentage points (95% CI: [0.104, 0.154], p < 0.001), reflecting the difficulty of jointly predicting both pitch type and location simultaneously.

**Model 3 vs. Model 4** (Basic vs. Separate - Combined Approximated): Model 3 outperformed Model 4 by 28.04 percentage points (95% CI: [0.255, 0.305], p < 0.001), representing the largest performance gap in any comparison involving Model 4 and underscoring that requiring simultaneous correctness on both type and zone dramatically reduces overall accuracy.

**Model 3 vs. Model 5** (Basic vs. Interaction): Model 3 outperformed Model 5 by 39.26 percentage points (95% CI: [0.366, 0.419], p < 0.001), the largest performance gap observed in any comparison and highlighting the severe limitations of the joint type-zone interaction approach.

**Model 4 vs. Model 5** (Separate - Combined Approximated vs. Interaction): Model 4 outperformed Model 5 by 11.22 percentage points (95% CI: [0.085, 0.139], p < 0.001), indicating that even the approximated combined accuracy of the separate model meaningfully exceeds the interaction model's performance.

### Effect Size Analysis

Cohen's d values confirm that differences are both statistically detectable and practically meaningful across most comparisons. Model 1 vs. Model 2 yielded d = -0.232, a small-to-medium effect indicating that while batter handedness contributes statistically, its practical impact is modest. Model 1 vs. Model 3 (d = -1.011) and Model 2 vs. Model 3 (d = -0.853) both produced large effect sizes, confirming that the addition of count and location information yields substantial real-world improvements. Model 3 vs. Model 4 (d = 1.122) and Model 3 vs. Model 5 (d = 3.413) produced the largest effect sizes, underscoring that Model 3 dramatically outperforms both joint-prediction approaches. Model 4 vs. Model 5 yielded d = 0.428, a medium effect, suggesting that while both approaches struggle with joint prediction, the separate model's approximated combined accuracy meaningfully exceeds the interaction model. Models 1 and 2 versus Model 4 both produced large effect sizes (d = 0.561 and d = 0.676 respectively), reflecting that even simple models outperform the joint prediction approach on a combined accuracy basis.

## Pitcher-Specific Performance

```{r}
pitcher_pitch_counts <- pitch_data1 %>%
  count(player_name, name = "total_pitches")

pitcher_performance <- all_accuracies %>%
  filter(model_type == "Combined") %>%
  group_by(pitcher) %>%
  summarise(
    n_models = n(),
    mean_accuracy = mean(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_accuracy = sd(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    min_accuracy = min(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_accuracy = max(accuracy, na.rm = TRUE),
    range_accuracy = max_accuracy - min_accuracy,
    .groups = "drop") %>%
  left_join(pitcher_pitch_counts, by = c("pitcher" = "player_name")) %>%
  arrange(desc(mean_accuracy))

top_10_pitchers <- pitcher_performance %>%
  filter(total_pitches >= 500) %>%
  head(10)

knitr::kable(top_10_pitchers, col.names = c("Pitcher ID", "N Models", "Mean Accuracy", "SD", "Min Acc", "Max Acc", "Range", "Total Pitches"), digits = 4, caption = "Top 10 Most Predictable Pitchers (Highest Mean Accuracy)")
```

Table 4.2 presents the ten most predictable pitchers in the dataset with a minimum of 500 pitches thrown, ranked by mean accuracy across all models. Tommy Kahnle leads with 70.26% mean accuracy, followed by Tim Hill (67.56%) and Kenley Jansen (64.25%). Notably, this list is dominated by relief pitchers as Kahnle, Jansen, Hill, Rogers, Clase, and Johnson are all bullpen arms, while Pomeranz, Mattson, Palencia, and Sabrowski are also primarily relievers. This pattern is likely not coincidental. Relief pitchers typically have narrower pitch repertoires than starters, often relying heavily on one or two primary pitches, which makes their selection patterns more systematic and therefore more predictable to a statistical model. Additionally, relief pitchers frequently enter games in high-leverage, specific situations as closers like Clase and Jansen are often deployed in defined roles which may further limit their pitch selection in predictable ways.

The standard deviations for most pitchers in this group are notably high, ranging from 0.2197 (Clase) to 0.3099 (Jansen), indicating that accuracy varies considerably depending on which model is used. This suggests that while these pitchers are genuinely predictable, the degree to which any given model captures their patterns depends heavily on model specification. Even so, the minimum accuracies for pitchers like Kahnle (25.71%) and Jansen (17.78%) show that not all models succeed equally, and the approximated Model 4 combined accuracy likely drives these lower bounds given its multiplicative penalty.

```{r}
bottom_10_pitchers <- tail(pitcher_performance, 10)
knitr::kable(bottom_10_pitchers, col.names = c("Pitcher ID", "N Models", "Mean Accuracy", "SD", "Min Acc", "Max Acc", "Range", "Total Pitches"), digits = 4, caption = "Top 10 Least Predictable Pitchers (Lowest Mean Accuracy)")
```

Table 4.3 presents the ten least predictable pitchers, all of whom are starting pitchers with substantial pitch counts ranging from 1,160 (Darvish) to 2,893 (Alcantara) pitches in the dataset. This stands in direct contrast to the most predictable group and reinforces the relief pitcher vs. starter dynamic observed above. Seth Lugo (22.65%), Yu Darvish (22.88%), and Michael Lorenzen (23.53%) show the lowest mean accuracy values, barely exceeding the random guessing baseline for a multi-class outcome. The presence of accomplished, experienced starters in this group like Darvish, Sandy Alcantara, Walker Buehler, and Cal Quantrill among them, suggests that elite starting pitchers are genuinely difficult to model, likely because they maintain diverse repertoires, adjust sequencing based on batter tendencies, and deliberately avoid falling into predictable patterns across a long outing.

The accuracy ranges for unpredictable pitchers are strikingly narrow compared to the most predictable group. Darvish's accuracy spans only 14.11 percentage points (17.54% to 31.65%), and Lugo's spans just 17.72 percentage points (11.76% to 29.47%), indicating that no model performs well for these pitchers regardless of specification. This consistency in poor performance across all four models suggests that these pitchers' unpredictability is a genuine characteristic of their approach rather than a limitation any particular model can overcome. Taken together, these two tables suggest that the most meaningful predictor of pitcher predictability in this dataset may not be age or experience, but rather role as relief pitchers with defined, narrow repertoires are systematically more predictable than starters who must vary their approach across many batters and innings.

```{r fig.cap="Distribution of Mean Accuracy Across Pitchers"}
ggplot(pitcher_performance, aes(x = mean_accuracy)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.02, fill = "#3498DB", color = "black", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = mean(mean_accuracy)), color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = mean(pitcher_performance$mean_accuracy), y = Inf, label = paste("Mean =", round(mean(pitcher_performance$mean_accuracy), 3)), vjust = 2, color = "red", fontface = "bold") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Mean Accuracy Across Pitchers", subtitle = "Average accuracy for each pitcher across all models", x = "Mean Accuracy", y = "Number of Pitchers") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14))
```

Figure 4.3 presents a histogram of mean accuracy across pitchers, where each pitcher's mean represents their average accuracy across all models for which they have predictions. The overall mean accuracy across all pitchers is 48.09% (median = 45.60%, SD = 13.53%), indicating substantial diversity in pitcher predictability.

The distribution appears approximately normal with slight right-skew, centered around 45-50% accuracy. Approximately 60% of pitchers fall within one standard deviation of the mean (34.5% to 61.6% accuracy). This relatively tight clustering around the middle of the distribution suggests that most pitchers exhibit moderate predictability as neither extremely systematic nor completely random in their pitch selection patterns. The right tail extends to several pitchers achieving mean accuracy above 80%, while the left tail includes pitchers below 30%, reflecting genuine differences in how pitchers approach sequencing.

```{r}
cor_test <- cor.test(pitcher_performance$mean_accuracy, pitcher_performance$sd_accuracy)
cat("Correlation between mean accuracy and SD:", round(cor_test$estimate, 4),
    "(p-value:", round(cor_test$p.value, 4), ")\n")
```

The correlation between mean accuracy and standard deviation across pitchers is 0.566 (p < 0.001), indicating a moderate positive relationship: more predictable pitchers tend to show greater variation across models. This pattern makes intuitive sense as when clear patterns exist, different models may capture different aspects of those patterns, leading to varying performance. When no clear patterns exist, all models perform poorly and similarly, yielding low standard deviation. This finding confirms that model choice matters primarily when systematic behavior exists to be modeled.

## Model Complexity vs. Performance

```{r fig.cap="Model Efficiency - Accuracy per Complexity Unit"}
model_complexity <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Model 1: Simple",
            "Model 2: Simple + Stand",
            "Model 3: Basic",
            "Model 4: Separate - Combined (Approximated)",
            "Model 5: Interaction"),
  Num_Features = c(3, 4, 7, 7, 10),
  Complexity_Score = c(1, 2, 4, 5, 8))

complexity_performance <- model_complexity %>%
  left_join(
    overall_model_stats %>%
      filter(!grepl("Zone Only", model_combined)) %>%
      filter(!grepl("Type Only", model_combined)) %>%
      select(model_combined, mean_accuracy),
    by = c("Model" = "model_combined")) %>%
  mutate(efficiency = mean_accuracy / Complexity_Score)

ggplot(complexity_performance, aes(x = reorder(Model, efficiency), y = efficiency, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.8, width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = sprintf("%.4f", efficiency)), hjust = -0.1, size = 4, fontface = "bold") +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "Model Efficiency: Accuracy per Complexity Unit", subtitle = "Higher values = better performance relative to complexity", x = NULL, y = "Accuracy / Complexity Score") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14), legend.position = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)))
```

Figure 4.4 presents model efficiency, calculated as mean accuracy divided by complexity score. Complexity scores were assigned based on the number of distinct predictor features and overall model structure: Model 1 (3 features) = complexity 1, Model 2 (4 features) = complexity 2, Model 3 (7 features) = complexity 4, Model 4 (7 features, two separate models) = complexity 5, and Model 5 (10 features, joint outcome) = complexity 8. Model 1 achieves the highest efficiency score (0.4720), indicating the best performance relative to its complexity. Despite its lower absolute accuracy (47.20%), its minimal complexity yields a strong efficiency ratio. Model 2 shows moderate efficiency (0.2487), while Model 3 achieves an efficiency of 0.1559 despite its highest absolute pitch-type accuracy. Model 4's approximated combined efficiency (0.0686) reflects the compounding penalty of requiring simultaneous correctness of two predictions. Model 5 achieves the lowest efficiency score (0.0289), confirming that its complexity investment yields almost no return in predictive accuracy.

This analysis highlights a fundamental tradeoff: Model 3 achieves the best absolute accuracy for pitch type prediction (62.36%) but requires substantial complexity, while Model 1 achieves moderate accuracy (47.20%) with minimal complexity. Model 4's purpose with jointly predicting both type and zone, introduces an intrinsic accuracy cost that its efficiency score reflects. For practical applications where real-time implementation is critical and interpretability is valued, Model 1's high efficiency may favor it despite lower accuracy. For applications where maximum pitch type accuracy is key and computational resources are available, Model 3's superior absolute performance justifies its complexity.

**Recommendations:**

- **For Maximum Accuracy**: Model 3 (62.36% accuracy), with large effect sizes justifying the added complexity
- **For Best Efficiency**: Model 1 (47.20% accuracy), optimal for real-time implementation
- **For Joint Type and Zone Prediction**: Model 4 Separate (34.32% approximated combined accuracy), the only model designed for this purpose
- **Avoid**: Model 5 (23.10% accuracy), which exhibits catastrophically poor performance at the highest complexity cost

# Discussion

This chapter interprets the findings presented in the Results section, discusses their implications for baseball analytics and practice, acknowledges limitations, and identifies directions for future research.

## Key Findings Summary

This research developed and evaluated five multinomial logistic regression model specifications for predicting pitch sequences in Major League Baseball. Analysis of 712,528 pitches from the 2025 MLB season across 767 pitchers yielded several key findings.

First, Model 3 (Basic) achieved the highest prediction accuracy for pitch type at 62.36%, substantially outperforming simpler alternatives. This comprehensive model, which incorporates count information, previous pitch types, previous pitch locations, and batter handedness, demonstrates that pitch selection is primarily driven by game state, particularly the count, rather than purely by sequential patterns.

Second, simple models achieved adequate but lower performance. Model 1 reached 47.20% accuracy and Model 2 improved to 49.75%, both substantially exceeding random guessing baselines of 30–35%. These results demonstrate that pitch sequencing patterns alone contain meaningful predictive information. The 2.55 percentage point improvement from adding handedness validates platoon considerations, though count information contributes more substantially (12.62 additional points from Model 2 to Model 3).

Third, Model 5 (Interaction) failed catastrophically, achieving only 23.10% accuracy which was worse than random guessing for most pitchers. This failure showed fundamental constraints on model complexity when outcome categories increase. The joint modeling of pitch type and location created 100+ distinct outcome categories, leading to severe data sparsity that prevented reliable parameter estimation.

Fourth, pitcher predictability varies enormously, with mean accuracy ranging from approximately 25% to over 70% among pitchers with at least 500 pitches thrown. This spread is strongly associated with pitcher role rather than age or experience. Relief pitchers with narrow repertoires, such as Tommy Kahnle and Kenley Jansen, dominate the most predictable group, while experienced starting pitchers with diverse arsenals, such as Yu Darvish and Seth Lugo, occupy the least predictable group. This pattern suggests that strategic unpredictability among starters may represent a developed skill rather than merely a failure to establish patterns.

Finally, statistical testing confirmed that performance differences are both significant and meaningful. ANOVA revealed overwhelming evidence of differences across models (F(4, 3659) = 483.2, p < 2×10^-16^), while effect size analysis confirmed large practical differences: Model 3 versus Model 1 yielded d = -1.011 (large effect), while Model 3 versus Model 5 produced d = 3.413 (enormous effect).

## Interpretation

### Why Model 3 Dominates

Model 3's superior performance validates the theoretical framework emphasizing count-dependent pitch selection as baseball's primary strategic dimension. When pitchers face unfavorable counts (more balls than strikes), strategic imperatives force them toward reliable strike-throwing pitches; typically fastballs. Conversely, favorable counts grant freedom to deploy full arsenals, including pitches that might miss the strike zone. These count-driven patterns create predictable behavior that Model 3 exploits by learning pitcher-specific count strategies. For example, how aggressively each pitcher leans on fastballs when behind, how extensively they attack with breaking balls when ahead, and how their sequencing patterns interact with count state.

Model 3's broad accuracy distribution across pitchers reveals that its value depends heavily on pitcher type. For relief pitchers with systematic, count-based strategies and narrow repertoires, it provides substantial advantages. For starting pitchers who deliberately vary their approach across many batters and innings, its additional complexity yields comparatively less benefit, though it still outperforms simpler models on average.

### Why Simple Models Perform Adequately

Models 1 and 2's respectable performance (47-50% accuracy) demonstrates that pitch sequencing patterns exist independently of count considerations. Baseball conventional wisdom about "setting up" hitters by using pitch sequences to disrupt timing and create deception, finds empirical support in these models' above-baseline accuracy. The simple models' narrow, concentrated accuracy distributions indicate consistent performance across diverse pitcher types, suggesting that basic sequencing patterns like fastballs followed by breaking balls, breaking balls in clusters, systematic first-pitch tendencies, occur with moderate regularity across the league regardless of individual pitcher characteristics.

Model 2's modest improvement over Model 1 (2.55 points) through adding handedness confirms platoon effects while revealing their secondary importance relative to count. Pitchers will adjust arsenals based on batter handedness, but these adjustments represent refinements rather than primary determinants of pitch selection. For applications requiring rapid computation, easy interpretation, or deployment with limited data infrastructure, these models offer viable alternatives despite lower absolute accuracy.

### Why the Interaction Model Failed

Model 5's catastrophic failure (23.10% accuracy) reveals fundamental limits on model complexity in the presence of data sparsity. With 7-10 pitch types and 14 zones, potentially 98-140 distinct type-zone combinations exist. Individual pitchers produce 80-100 combinations over a season, but many occur only 5-10 times which is insufficient for stable parameter estimation. Maximum likelihood estimation struggles with rare outcome categories, yielding parameter estimates that are essentially random rather than systematically related to predictors.

The increase of parameters worsens this problem. Each predictor requires a coefficient for each outcome category, creating potentially thousands of parameters to estimate from only 2,000-3,000 pitch observations per pitcher. This parameter-to-observation ratio violates fundamental statistical principles about sample size requirements for stable estimation. The theoretical motivation for joint type-location modeling was sound as pitch type and location clearly relate, but practical implementation encountered insurmountable obstacles. This failure demonstrates that more information and refined relationship modeling can backfire when complexity increases faster than data availability.

### Pitcher-Specific Patterns

The variation in predictability across pitchers reflects genuine strategic diversity rather than simple sampling variation. The most striking finding is the role-based divide between relief pitchers and starters. Relief pitchers dominate the most predictable group, likely because they carry narrower pitch repertoires, enter games in defined high-leverage situations, and often rely on one or two elite pitches rather than sequencing across a full arsenal. Closers like Emmanuel Clase and Kenley Jansen are deployed in specific contexts that constrain their pitch selection in ways statistical models can exploit. Conversely, starting pitchers dominate the least predictable group. Elite veterans like Yu Darvish and Sandy Alcantara who both have substantial pitch counts confirmed this is not a sample size artifact, as they maintain diverse repertoires and adjust sequencing dynamically across a full outing, making their behavior far harder to model. The presence of these accomplished starters among the least predictable pitchers supports the interpretation that unpredictability is a cultivated competitive skill rather than a random characteristic.

The moderate positive correlation between mean accuracy and standard deviation across models (r = 0.566) provides additional insight. When clear patterns exist, different modeling approaches capture different pattern aspects with varying success, yielding high standard deviation. When no clear patterns exist, all models fail similarly, producing low standard deviation despite low mean accuracy. This confirms that model choice matters primarily when organized behavior exists.

## Practical Applications

### Selective Implementation by Opponent

Rather than deploying predictive models universally, teams could implement them selectively based on both opponent predictability and pitcher role. Pre-game analysis identifying relief pitchers where Model 3 accuracy exceeds 60-70% would indicate the most worthwhile targets for real-time prediction, while starting pitchers, who tend to be less predictable and adjust dynamically across outings, may warrant a more conservative deployment threshold.

### Pre-Game Scouting Enhancement

Models could generate comprehensive scouting reports before games, condensed into simple decision rules that hitters memorize. For example, "in two-strike counts after throwing two consecutive fastballs, Pitcher X throws sliders 65% of the time." These memorable patterns could allow hitters to prepare mentally without requiring technological assistance during at-bats. Transforming complex statistical models into instinctively applicable rules of thumb could be useful to comply with current MLB in-game technology rules.

### Pitcher Self-Analysis and Development

Pitchers and pitching coaches could use these models diagnostically to assess their own predictability. A pitcher discovering they are highly predictable (Model 1 achieves 70%+ accuracy) might intentionally introduce more randomness into their sequencing. Conversely, a developing pitcher struggling with consistency might benefit from becoming more systematic, establishing reliable sequencing patterns that allow better execution planning. This self-analysis inverts the traditional use case. As rather than exploiting opponent predictability, pitchers use the model to evaluate and improve their own strategic approach.

## Limitations

### Data and Temporal Limitations

This research analyzed only the 2025 MLB season, providing substantial data (712,528 pitches) but that makes it impossible to tell if the findings hold up over time. Do individual pitchers maintain consistent sequencing patterns across multiple seasons, or do they evolve their approaches over time? Single-season analysis cannot address these questions about pattern persistence and strategic evolution. The pitcher-specific modeling approach also creates sample size challenges for pitchers near minimum thresholds, where parameter estimates may be less stable than for high-workload pitchers with 3,000+ pitches. Additionally, the decision to filter pitcher-specific performance tables to pitchers with a minimum of 500 pitches excludes a portion of the dataset from individual-level analysis. While this threshold ensures more stable model estimates, it means that findings about pitcher predictability reflect only those with sufficient workload and may not generalize to pitchers at the margins of MLB rosters.

### Methodological Limitations

Classification accuracy treats all prediction errors equally: predicting a curveball when a slider was thrown costs the same as predicting a curveball when a fastball was thrown, despite these errors having very different strategic implications. Alternative metrics like logarithmic loss or Brier score could provide more refined assessment by considering probability distributions. Additionally, the absence of formal cross-validation in this research means absolute accuracy figures may be slightly optimistic, as models were evaluated on the same data used for training. However, since all models received identical treatment, relative performance comparisons remain valid.

The static nature of the models being trained on full-season data and applied uniformly, fail to account for within-season dynamics. Pitchers adjust approaches based on effectiveness, opponent adaptations, or physical changes such as fatigue or minor injury. A model trained on April-September data may poorly predict behavior if a pitcher substantially alters their strategy late in the season or during the playoffs.

### Contextual Limitations

This research examines pitch selection in isolation from broader game context: score differential, base-out state, inning, bullpen availability, and defensive positioning. However, these all affect pitch selection but were excluded to preserve implementability. The analysis also treats all pitches as purely pitcher-driven, ignoring catchers' significant role in pitch calling. In modern MLB, catchers influence pitch selection substantially, particularly for younger pitchers who might defer more heavily to catcher judgment, meaning models may miss important catcher-pitcher dynamic effects.

## Future Research Directions

### Multi-Season Temporal Analysis

Analyzing 3-5 seasons of data would enable assessment of temporal stability in pitcher patterns and investigation of how individual pitchers' predictability evolves over careers. Multi-season analysis could also address whether models trained on past seasons successfully predict future seasons, and whether career-stage patterns emerge. Do rookie pitchers show high predictability that decreases as they develop more sophisticated sequencing strategies?

### Hierarchical and Bayesian Modeling

Rather than building completely separate models for each pitcher, hierarchical Bayesian approaches could allow pitchers to "borrow strength" from each other while preserving individual differences. Pitchers with similar characteristics like comparable arsenals, similar roles, comparable experience levels, likely share some strategic patterns. This approach would improve accuracy for pitchers with limited data while maintaining flexibility for well-characterized pitchers. Bayesian methods also measure uncertainty more rigorously, producing a range of possible outcomes that show how confident we can be in each prediction and whether that confidence is high enough to act on.

### Alternative Modeling Frameworks

While multinomial logistic regression worked well, other approaches are worth exploring. Recurrent neural networks could better capture patterns across longer sequences of pitches than the two-pitch look back used here. Hidden Markov Models might uncover hidden strategic tendencies such as whether a pitcher is in an aggressive or cautious mode which could shape their pitch selection. Reinforcement learning could model pitchers as agents who gradually learn the best strategies through experience. Although early testing showed Random Forests and XGBoost offering no real improvement over logistic regression, more advanced combinations of multiple methods might still outperform any single model while also giving better estimates of prediction confidence.

### Substantive Baseball Research Questions

Several substantive questions emerge from this work. Does pitcher predictability correlate with performance metrics like ERA, WHIP, or WAR? And if so, in which direction? Do hitters adjust their approach against predictable pitchers differently than against unpredictable ones, and do patient hitters exploit predictability more effectively than aggressive hitters? Could changes in predictability patterns serve as an early injury indicator, since a pitcher who suddenly becomes predictable may be favoring certain pitches due to discomfort? Finally, controlled field experiments in minor leagues could test whether predictive models actually improve offensive performance when deployed, moving beyond correlational evidence to causal evaluation of model value.

# Conclusion

This research demonstrates that pitch sequences in Major League Baseball exhibit meaningful and exploitable predictability through multinomial logistic regression models incorporating lagged variables. The comprehensive model achieves 62.36% accuracy for pitch type prediction which is a substantial improvement over baseline expectations and a 15-percentage-point advantage over simpler models.

Four key insights emerge from this work. First, pitch selection is fundamentally driven by game state, particularly the count, rather than by simple sequential patterns alone. Second, pitcher predictability varies enormously across individuals and is strongly associated with pitcher role like relief pitchers with narrow repertoires who are systematically more predictable than starting pitchers who vary their approach across full outings. Third, model complexity must be carefully calibrated to available data, as demonstrated by the catastrophic failure of the interaction model when outcome categories expaned beyond what the data could support. Fourth, jointly predicting pitch type and location simultaneously introduces a compounding accuracy penalty, with the approximated combined accuracy of Model 4 (34.32%) reflecting the difficulty of requiring correctness on two dimensions at once.

These findings have practical implications for baseball operations. Teams could deploy models selectively by prioritizing relief pitchers and high-predictability opponents, use them diagnostically for pitcher self-assessment, or integrate predictions into pre-game scouting reports. However, implementation must account for accuracy ceilings leaving 35–40% of pitch type predictions incorrect even under the best model specification.

The methodological contribution extends beyond baseball. The successful integration of categorical lagged variables into multinomial logistic regression provides a framework applicable to diverse sequential categorical prediction problems in healthcare, customer analytics, education, and other domains where behavior unfolds in structured sequences.

Substantial opportunities remain for future research, including multi-season analysis to assess temporal stability, hierarchical Bayesian approaches to improve estimates for low-workload pitchers, and field experiments testing whether predictions improve offensive performance when actually deployed. As baseball continues integrating statistical modeling into strategy, approaches balancing predictive performance against practical implementability and interpretability will prove most valuable.

The question is not whether pitch sequences can be predicted, but rather how much prediction accuracy provides sufficient value to justify the analytical investment, cognitive load, and potential strategic adaptations that widespread deployment would entail. This research establishes that prediction is feasible and achieves non-trivial accuracy and that the most productive targets for deployment are relief pitchers whose defined roles and narrow repertoires make them systematically more transparent to statistical modeling.

## Appendix A: Model Building Code

### Model 1: Simple Model

```{r eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=30)}
build_simple_pitcher_model <- function(pitcher_data) {
  tryCatch({
    model <- multinom(
      pitch_type ~ prev_pitch_type_1 + prev_pitch_type_2 + pitch_number,
      data = pitcher_data,
      maxit = 500,
      trace = FALSE
    )
    return(model)
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(NULL)
  })
}

pitcher_simple_models <- list()

for (pitcher in pitchers_sufficient_data) {
  cat("\nBuilding simple model for:", pitcher)

  pitcher_data <- pitch_data_simple %>%
    filter(player_name == pitcher)

  model <- build_simple_pitcher_model(pitcher_data)

  if (!is.null(model)) {
    pitcher_simple_models[[pitcher]] <- model
    cat(" - Success")
  } else {
    cat(" - Failed")
  }
}

cat("\n\nTotal simple models built:", length(pitcher_simple_models), "\n")

evaluate_simple_pitcher_model <- function(pitcher_name, model, pitcher_data) {
  tryCatch({
    predictions <- predict(model, newdata = pitcher_data, type = "class")

    accuracy <- mean(as.character(predictions) == as.character(pitcher_data$pitch_type), na.rm = TRUE)

    conf_matrix <- tryCatch({
      pred_char <- as.character(predictions)
      actual_char <- as.character(pitcher_data$pitch_type)

      common_levels <- sort(unique(c(pred_char, actual_char)))

      confusionMatrix(
        factor(pred_char, levels = common_levels),
        factor(actual_char, levels = common_levels)
      )
    }, error = function(e) {
      NULL
    })

    return(list(
      pitcher = pitcher_name,
      accuracy = accuracy,
      confusion_matrix = conf_matrix,
      error = NULL
    ))
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(list(
      pitcher = pitcher_name,
      accuracy = NA,
      confusion_matrix = NULL,
      error = e$message
    ))
  })
}

simple_model_evaluations <- list()

for (pitcher in names(pitcher_simple_models)) {
  pitcher_data <- pitch_data_simple %>%
    filter(player_name == pitcher)

  eval <- evaluate_simple_pitcher_model(pitcher, pitcher_simple_models[[pitcher]], pitcher_data)
  simple_model_evaluations[[pitcher]] <- eval
}

simple_accuracy_summary <- data.frame(
  pitcher = names(simple_model_evaluations),
  accuracy = sapply(simple_model_evaluations, function(x) x$accuracy),
  error = sapply(simple_model_evaluations, function(x) {
    if (!is.null(x$error)) return(x$error) else return(NA)
  })) %>%
  arrange(desc(accuracy))
print(simple_accuracy_summary)

cat("\n\nSimple Model Statistics:\n")
cat("Models with errors:", sum(!is.na(simple_accuracy_summary$error)), "\n")
cat("Models successful:", sum(is.na(simple_accuracy_summary$error) & !is.na(simple_accuracy_summary$accuracy)), "\n")
cat("Mean accuracy:", round(mean(simple_accuracy_summary$accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("Median accuracy:", round(median(simple_accuracy_summary$accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("Min accuracy:", round(min(simple_accuracy_summary$accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
cat("Max accuracy:", round(max(simple_accuracy_summary$accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), 3), "\n")
```

### Model 2: Simple Model with Batter Handness (Stand)

```{r eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=30)}
build_simple_pitcher_model <- function(pitcher_data) {
  tryCatch({
    model <- multinom(
      pitch_type ~ prev_pitch_type_1 + prev_pitch_type_2 + pitch_number + stand,
      data = pitcher_data,
      maxit = 500,
      trace = FALSE
    )
    return(model)
```

### Model 5: Interaction Model

```{r eval=FALSE, echo=TRUE, tidy=TRUE, tidy.opts=list(width.cutoff=30)}
build_pitcher_interaction_model <- function(pitcher_data) {
  tryCatch({
    n_combinations <- n_distinct(pitcher_data$pitch_type_zone)
    n_pitches <- nrow(pitcher_data)

    cat(" | Combinations:", n_combinations, "| Pitches:", n_pitches)

    if (n_pitches / n_combinations < 5) {
      cat(" - Too sparse")
      return(NULL)
    }

    combination_counts <- pitcher_data %>%
      count(pitch_type_zone) %>%
      filter(n >= 3)

    pitcher_data_filtered <- pitcher_data %>%
      filter(pitch_type_zone %in% combination_counts$pitch_type_zone) %>%
      mutate(pitch_type_zone = droplevels(pitch_type_zone))

    cat(" | Filtered to:", n_distinct(pitcher_data_filtered$pitch_type_zone), "combinations")

    if (nrow(pitcher_data_filtered) < 50) {
      cat(" - Insufficient data after filtering")
      return(NULL)
    }

    model <- multinom(
      pitch_type_zone ~ prev_pitch_type_1 + prev_zone_1 +
                        balls + strikes + stand,
      data = pitcher_data_filtered,
      maxit = 1000,
      trace = FALSE,
      MaxNWts = 5000
    )
    return(model)
  }, error = function(e) {
    cat(" - Error:", e$message)
    return(NULL)
  })
}

pitcher_interaction_models <- list()

for (pitcher in pitchers_sufficient_data) {
  cat("\nBuilding interaction model for:", pitcher)

  pitcher_data <- pitch_data_features %>%
    filter(player_name == pitcher)

  model <- build_pitcher_interaction_model(pitcher_data)

  if (!is.null(model)) {
    pitcher_interaction_models[[pitcher]] <- model
    cat(" - Success")
  } else {
    cat(" - Failed")
  }
}

cat("\n\nTotal interaction models built:", length(pitcher_interaction_models))

evaluate_pitcher_interaction_model <- function(pitcher_name, model, pitcher_data) {
  tryCatch({
    predictions <- predict(model, newdata = pitcher_data, type = "class")

    accuracy <- mean(as.character(predictions) == as.character(pitcher_data$pitch_type_zone), na.rm = TRUE)

    pred_split <- str_split_fixed(as.character(predictions), "_", 2)
    actual_split <- str_split_fixed(as.character(pitcher_data$pitch_type_zone), "_", 2)

    type_accuracy <- mean(pred_split[,1] == actual_split[,1], na.rm = TRUE)
    zone_accuracy <- mean(pred_split[,2] == actual_split[,2], na.rm = TRUE)

    conf_matrix <- tryCatch({
      pred_char <- as.character(predictions)
      actual_char <- as.character(pitcher_data$pitch_type_zone)
      common_levels <- sort(unique(c(pred_char, actual_char)))

      confusionMatrix(
        factor(pred_char, levels = common_levels),
        factor(actual_char, levels = common_levels)
      )
    }, error = function(e) NULL)

    return(list(
      pitcher = pitcher_name,
      combined_accuracy = accuracy,
      type_accuracy = type_accuracy,
      zone_accuracy = zone_accuracy,
      confusion_matrix = conf_matrix,
      error = NULL
    ))
  }, error = function(e) {
    return(list(
      pitcher = pitcher_name,
      combined_accuracy = NA,
      type_accuracy = NA,
      zone_accuracy = NA,
      confusion_matrix = NULL,
      error = e$message
    ))
  })
}

interaction_model_evaluations <- list()

for (pitcher in names(pitcher_interaction_models)) {
  pitcher_data <- pitch_data_features %>%
    filter(player_name == pitcher)

  eval <- evaluate_pitcher_interaction_model(pitcher, pitcher_interaction_models[[pitcher]], pitcher_data)
  interaction_model_evaluations[[pitcher]] <- eval
}

interaction_accuracy_summary <- data.frame(
  pitcher = names(interaction_model_evaluations),
  combined_accuracy = sapply(interaction_model_evaluations, function(x) x$combined_accuracy),
  type_accuracy = sapply(interaction_model_evaluations, function(x) x$type_accuracy),
  zone_accuracy = sapply(interaction_model_evaluations, function(x) x$zone_accuracy),
  error = sapply(interaction_model_evaluations, function(x) {
    if (!is.null(x$error)) return(x$error) else return(NA)
  })) %>%
  arrange(desc(combined_accuracy))
print(interaction_accuracy_summary)

cat("\n\n=== INTERACTION MODEL PERFORMANCE ===\n")
cat("Models with errors:", sum(!is.na(interaction_accuracy_summary$error)), "\n")
cat("Models successful:", sum(is.na(interaction_accuracy_summary$error) & !is.na(interaction_accuracy_summary$combined_accuracy)), "\n")
cat("Mean combined accuracy:", round(mean(interaction_accuracy_summary$combined_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), 4), "\n")
cat("Mean type accuracy (from interaction):", round(mean(interaction_accuracy_summary$type_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), 4), "\n")
cat("Mean zone accuracy (from interaction):", round(mean(interaction_accuracy_summary$zone_accuracy, na.rm = TRUE), 4), "\n")
```
